reference_title: California Trenching and Shoring Manual (Caltrans, June 2011, Revision 2 - July 2025)

sections.title: Shoring Types and Shoring Movement/Loading
sections.summary: Shoring is unrestrained (non-gravity cantilevered soldier-pile or sheet-pile walls relying on passive resistance and member bending; economical to ~18 ft) or restrained (braced/anchored walls with struts, rakers, or ground anchors; feasible to ~80 ft). Shoring that cannot tolerate any movement should be designed for at-rest pressure; shoring that can move away from the soil should be designed for active pressure. The active/passive variation requires lateral wall movement (Table 4-1, Clough 1991); far more movement mobilizes full passive than active. Soil nail and MSE walls are excluded.
sections.body: Shoring systems are unrestrained (non-gravity cantilevered walls) or restrained (braced or anchored). Unrestrained systems are partially embedded soldier piles or continuous sheet piles relying on the passive resistance of the foundation material and member moment capacity; economical height is generally limited to ~18 ft. Restrained systems (Figure 4-1) add one or more levels of braces, rakers, or anchors (or trench struts) and are feasible to ~80 ft. Soil Nail and MSE walls are not included. Shoring systems that cannot tolerate any movement should be designed for at-rest lateral earth pressure; shoring systems which can move away from the soil mass should be designed for active earth pressure conditions depending on the magnitude of the tolerable movement. The movement to reach minimum active or maximum passive pressure is a function of wall height and soil type; typical mobilizing movements (Delta/H, Delta = movement of the top of wall by tilting or lateral translation, H = wall height) are in Table 4-1 (Clough 1991): active / passive 0.001 / 0.01 dense sand, 0.002 / 0.02 medium dense sand, 0.004 / 0.04 loose sand, 0.002 / 0.02 compacted silt, 0.01 / 0.05 compacted lean clay and compacted fat clay, and a significant amount of movement is needed to mobilize full passive pressure (Figure 4-2).
key_points: Unrestrained = non-gravity cantilever (soldier/sheet pile), economical to ~18 ft
Restrained = braced/anchored (struts, rakers, ground anchors), feasible to ~80 ft
Shoring that cannot tolerate movement should be designed for at-rest pressure; shoring that can move away, for active pressure
Mobilizing movement delta/H from Table 4-1 (Clough 1991)
Full passive pressure needs far more movement than active
Soil Nail and MSE walls are excluded from this manual

sections.title: Developing Earth Pressures for Granular Soil (Rankine, Coulomb, At-Rest)
sections.summary: Horizontal stress sigma_h = sigma_v*K = gamma*h*K (Eq. 4-3-1), K = Ka, Kp or K0; the resultant P = (1/2)*sigma_h*h (Eq. 4-3-2) acts at h/3. Rankine (smooth vertical wall): Ka = tan^2(45 - phi/2) (Eq. 4-3-11), Kp = tan^2(45 + phi/2) (Eq. 4-3-12), sloping-backfill forms Eqs. 4-3-16 and 4-3-19; the Rankine method should not be used for passive pressure when beta > 0. Coulomb adds wall friction delta (Table 4-2) but can give inaccurate passive results with a large back slope or wall friction, so it is also recommended not to use it for passive pressure. At-rest (may be taken as): K0 = (1 - sin phi)(1 - sin beta) NC, K0 = (1 - sin phi)*OCR^(sin phi) OC.
sections.body: Earth pressure methods in common use are Rankine (1857) and Coulomb (1776), both limit-equilibrium with an assumed planar surface; experiments show the sliding surface is not a plane but a curved surface (Figure 4-3, Terzaghi 1943); the Rankine and Coulomb theories lead to quite accurate results for the active earth pressure, but for the passive earth pressure they are accurate only for a backfill of clean, dry sand, which would lead to a low wall-interface friction angle. For level homogeneous backfill, sigma_h = sigma_v*K = gamma*h*K (Eq. 4-3-1) and the resultant P = (1/2)*sigma_h*h (Eq. 4-3-2) acts at h/3 above the base, h the height of the pressure surface from the ground surface to the base of the wall. At-rest coefficient (zero lateral strain): K0 = mu/(1-mu) (Eq. 4-3-13); for normally consolidated soils and vertical walls K0 may be taken as (1 - sin phi)(1 - sin beta) (Eq. 4-3-14); for over-consolidated soils, level backfill and a vertical wall, K0 may be taken as (1 - sin phi)*(OCR)^(sin phi) (Eq. 4-3-15); the at-rest equations are empirical. Rankine (smooth vertical frictionless wall): Ka = tan^2(45 - phi/2) (Eq. 4-3-11), Kp = tan^2(45 + phi/2) (Eq. 4-3-12); for a backfill slope beta, Ka = cos(beta)*[cos(beta) - sqrt(cos^2(beta) - cos^2(phi))]/[cos(beta) + sqrt(cos^2(beta) - cos^2(phi))] (Eq. 4-3-16), Pa = (1/2)(gamma)(h^2)(Ka) (Eq. 4-3-17), failure plane alpha = (45 + phi/2) - (1/2)[arcsin(sin beta/sin phi) - beta] (Eq. 4-3-18); Kp = cos(beta)*[cos(beta) + sqrt(cos^2(beta) - cos^2(phi))]/[cos(beta) - sqrt(cos^2(beta) - cos^2(phi))] (Eq. 4-3-19), Pp = (1/2)(gamma)(h^2)(Kp) (Eq. 4-3-20), alpha = (45 - phi/2) + (1/2)[arcsin(sin beta/sin phi) + beta] (Eq. 4-3-21). One should not use the Rankine method to calculate the passive earth pressure when the backfill angle is greater than zero (beta > 0): its Kp is identical for positive and negative slopes, which is clearly not correct (p. 4-12). If a large wall friction value can develop, the Rankine theory is not correct and will give less conservative results; its use is to be avoided for passive earth pressure (p. 4-16). Coulomb (rough wall, friction/adhesion delta, Eq. 4-3-22/4-3-24) accounts for wall friction (Table 4-2 typical delta) but assumes planar surfaces, so it gives only approximate results, with accuracy diminishing with increased depth, and for passive pressures it can give inaccurate results with a large back slope or wall friction angle; because of these limitations it is also recommended not to use Coulomb for the passive earth pressure (p. 4-16). Section 4-6 gives the Log-Spiral passive earth pressure.
key_points: sigma_h = gamma*h*K; triangular resultant P = 0.5*gamma*h^2*K acts at h/3 (Eq. 4-3-1, 4-3-2)
Rankine active: Ka = tan^2(45 - phi/2) (Eq. 4-3-11)
Rankine passive: Kp = tan^2(45 + phi/2) (Eq. 4-3-12); the Rankine method should not be used for passive pressure when beta > 0
Coulomb adds wall friction delta (Table 4-2); it is also recommended not to use Coulomb for passive pressure (large back slope or wall friction)
At-rest NC, vertical wall: K0 may be taken as (1 - sin phi)(1 - sin beta) (Eq. 4-3-14); the at-rest equations are empirical
At-rest OC: K0 = (1 - sin phi)*OCR^(sin phi) (Eq. 4-3-15)
Log-Spiral passive earth pressure: Section 4-6

equations.description: Triangular lateral earth pressure resultant P = 0.5*gamma*h^2*K, acting at h/3.
Rankine active coefficient Ka = tan^2(45 - phi/2).
Rankine passive coefficient Kp = tan^2(45 + phi/2).
At-rest coefficient for normally consolidated soil: K0 = (1 - sin phi)(1 - sin beta).
At-rest coefficient for over-consolidated soil: K0 = (1 - sin phi)*OCR^(sin phi).
Coulomb active coefficient Ka (with wall friction delta, slope beta, wall batter omega).

sections.title: Developing Earth Pressures for Cohesive Soil; Apparent Active Coefficient
sections.summary: Bell (1952) modified Rankine for cohesion: sigma_a = sigma_v*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka) and sigma_p = sigma_v*Kp + 2c*sqrt(Kp), sigma_v = gamma*z (Eqs. 4-4-6, 4-4-9). Setting sigma_a = gamma*h*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka) = 0 gives the tension crack depth hcr = 2c*sqrt(Ka)/(gamma*Ka) (Eq. 4-4-13); with water the crack fills and the hydrostatic pressure needs to be considered. For shoring supporting cohesive backfill hcr should be ignored and a modified full-height distribution used, with Kapparent = sigma_a/(gamma*h) >= 0.25 (Eq. 4-4-16); a design with Kapparent below 0.25 must have justification.
sections.body: Neither Coulomb nor Rankine explicitly include cohesion; Bell (1952) modified Rankine. For the active case sigma_a = sigma_v*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka) and for the passive case sigma_p = sigma_v*Kp + 2c*sqrt(Kp) (Eqs. 4-4-6 and 4-4-9, where sigma_v = gamma*z; Eqs. 4-4-5 and 4-4-8 write Ka and Kp as tan^2(45 - phi/2) and tan^2(45 + phi/2)). At depth h, sigma_a = gamma*h*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka) (Eq. 4-4-10) and Pa = (1/2)*gamma*h^2*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka)*(h) (Eq. 4-4-11); sigma_p = gamma*h*Kp + 2c*sqrt(Kp) (Eq. 4-4-14) and Pp = (1/2)*gamma*h^2*Kp + 2c*sqrt(Kp)*(h) (Eq. 4-4-15). The active stress is zero at a shallow depth and the soil is in tension above it; setting gamma*h*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka) = 0 (Eq. 4-4-12), the tension crack zone extends from the surface to depth hcr = 2c*sqrt(Ka)/(gamma*Ka) (Eq. 4-4-13, as printed; equal to 2c/(gamma*sqrt(Ka)); Figure 4-12), and when water is present the crack fills, adding hydrostatic pressure. Extreme caution is advised using the cohesion value c, because the induced stress is highly uncertain (shrink-swell, wet-dry, saturation). For shoring systems which support cohesive backfill, the height of the tension zone hcr should be ignored, as it is undeterminable when a crack develops and the cohesive tension in the soil is no longer present; a modified lateral earth pressure distribution acting along the entire wall height should be used (Figure 4-14). The base active stress sigma_a may be used provided it is not less than a minimum apparent active coefficient of 0.25 times the effective vertical stress (gamma*h). Because cohesion shifts the pressure diagram to a lower horizontal stress, a revised 'apparent active earth pressure coefficient' Kapparent = sigma_a/(gamma*h) is computed, and Kapparent must be >= 0.25 (Eq. 4-4-16). Any design with Kapparent < 0.25 must be justified (multiple lab tests for c, the excavation time frame, and other conditions).
key_points: Bell cohesive: sigma_a = sigma_v*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka); sigma_p = sigma_v*Kp + 2c*sqrt(Kp)
Tension crack depth hcr = 2c*sqrt(Ka)/(gamma*Ka) (Eq. 4-4-13), from gamma*h*Ka - 2c*sqrt(Ka) = 0
With water, the tension crack fills and the hydrostatic pressure needs to be considered (Figure 4-15)
For shoring, hcr should be ignored and a modified full-height distribution used (Figure 4-14)
Apparent active coefficient Kapparent = sigma_a/(gamma*h), must be >= 0.25 (Eq. 4-4-16)
A design with Kapparent < 0.25 must have justification (e.g. multiple lab tests for c, the excavation time frame, other conditions affecting c)

equations.description: Depth of the tension crack zone, as printed: hcr = 2c*sqrt(Ka)/(gamma*Ka) (= 2c/(gamma*sqrt(Ka))).
Apparent active earth pressure coefficient Kapparent = sigma_a/(gamma*h) >= 0.25.

sections.title: Estimating Maximum Allowable Embankment Slope Angle
sections.summary: Many natural slopes stand at a slope angle beta larger than phi because of cohesion c, but none of the earth pressure theories work when beta > phi, even in cohesive soil. Equations based on the ASCE Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering (February 1997) estimate the maximum allowable embankment slope angle for c-phi backfill: sin(beta) <= sin(phi) + (c/l)*cos(phi) (Eq. 4-5-1), with l from Eq. 4-5-2 and sigma_v = gamma*(H cos beta), sigma_x = gamma*(H cos^2 beta) (Eqs. 4-5-3, 4-5-4). Eq. 4-5-2 as printed is not dimensionally consistent.
sections.body: In nature, there are many stable slopes that have slope angles (beta) larger than the angles of internal friction (phi), due to the presence of cohesion (c). None of the earth pressure theories will work when the slope angle beta is larger than the friction angle phi, even if the shoring system is to be installed in cohesive soil. The Mohr circle representation of a c-phi backfill with beta <= phi is shown in Figure 4-16. The following equations are based on the ASCE Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering (February 1997) and are used to estimate the maximum allowable embankment slope angle for c-phi soil backfill: sin(beta) <= sin(phi) + (c/l)*cos(phi) (Eq. 4-5-1), where l = (1/cos^2(phi))*[sigma_x + (1/2)*sin(2 phi) - sqrt(sigma_v*(cos^2(beta) - cos^2(phi)) + sigma_x*[c*sin(2 phi)] + c^2*cos^2(phi))] (Eq. 4-5-2), sigma_v = gamma*(H cos beta) (Eq. 4-5-3) and sigma_x = gamma*(H cos^2 beta) (Eq. 4-5-4). Note: Eq. 4-5-2 is stored as printed (p. 4-22); as printed it is not dimensionally consistent (a pure number, (1/2) sin(2 phi), is added to the stress sigma_x, and under the root a stress is added to stress-squared terms). The sections that follow outline methods for shoring with sloping ground: the Active Trial Wedge method (4-5.01, Eq. 4-5-5, failure angle varied until Pa is a maximum), the Passive Trial Wedge method (4-5.02, Eq. 4-5-6, varied until Pp is a minimum) and Culmann's graphical solution for active earth pressure (4-5.03; Appendix A).
key_points: None of the earth pressure theories work when the slope angle beta exceeds the friction angle phi, even in cohesive soil
Cohesion c lets natural slopes stand steeper than phi
Max allowable slope estimate (ASCE JGGE Feb 1997): sin(beta) <= sin(phi) + (c/l)*cos(phi) (Eq. 4-5-1), l from Eq. 4-5-2
sigma_v = gamma*(H cos beta) (Eq. 4-5-3); sigma_x = gamma*(H cos^2 beta) (Eq. 4-5-4)
Eq. 4-5-2 as printed is not dimensionally consistent; it is stored as printed
Trial wedge methods: active, failure angle varied until Pa is a maximum (Eq. 4-5-5); passive, until Pp is a minimum (Eq. 4-5-6)

equations.description: Maximum allowable embankment slope angle for c-phi soil backfill: sin(beta) <= sin(phi) + (c/l)*cos(phi), l = (1/cos^2 phi)[sigma_x + (1/2) sin(2 phi) - sqrt(sigma_v(cos^2 beta - cos^2 phi) + sigma_x[c sin(2 phi)] + c^2 cos^2 phi)] (Eq. 4-5-2, as printed), sigma_v = gamma(H cos beta), sigma_x = gamma(H cos^2 beta) (Eqs. 4-5-3, 4-5-4).

sections.title: Log-Spiral Passive Earth Pressure (Caquot & Kerisel)
sections.summary: Rankine's theory should not be used for passive pressure on shoring because it does not account for wall friction; Coulomb's assumes a planar surface and gives increasingly erroneous passive values as wall friction delta increases, which could lead to unsafe designs. Kp for shoring in granular soils can be estimated with Figure 4-20 (Caquot & Kerisel 1948): initial Kp from phi and beta/phi, reduction factor R from delta/phi and phi (Matrix 4-1), Kp' = R x Kp. Other conditions: a trial wedge or logarithmic spiral procedure. Example: phi=32, beta/phi=0.84 -> Kp~19; delta/phi=0.44 -> R=0.679; Kp' = 13.
sections.body: A shoring system is stable when the active earth pressure on the high side is opposed by much higher passive earth pressure on the low side (Figure 4-3). The sliding surface for active earth pressure is practically a straight line, whereas a straight line cannot approximate the sliding surface for passive earth pressure (Appendix A compares the composite spiral-straight line and the full Log-Spiral analysis). Rankine's theory should not be used to calculate the passive earth pressure forces for a shoring system because it does not account for wall friction. Coulomb's theory accounts for wall friction delta but assumes a linear failure surface, so its passive force is in error and becomes increasingly erroneous as delta increases; it could lead to unsafe shoring designs because the calculated passive pressure would become higher than the soil could generate. Terzaghi (1943) suggested a logarithmic spiral combined with a straight line; Morrison and Ebeling (1995) a single arc of the logarithmic spiral. (Section 4-3.03, p. 4-16: the difference between the Log-Spiral and straight-line surfaces can be large and on the unsafe side for Coulomb passive pressures, especially when wall friction exceeds phi/3.) Kp for the shoring system in granular soils can be estimated using Figure 4-20 (Passive Earth Pressure Coefficient, Caquot & Kerisel 1948), which requires delta, beta and phi; its failure surface is a logarithmic spiral and a straight line. For conditions that deviate from those described in Figure 4-20, the passive pressure may be calculated using a trial procedure based on the trial wedge theory or a logarithmic spiral method. Procedure: (1) given delta, beta, phi; (2) calculate delta/phi and beta/phi; (3) determine initial Kp for beta/phi from Figure 4-20; (4) determine reduction factor R using delta/phi (table in the upper left of the chart; Matrix 4-1); (5) calculate final Kp' = R x Kp. Example: delta = 14 deg, beta = 27 deg, phi = 32 deg; beta/phi = 0.84; interpolating between the +0.8 and +1 lines gives initial Kp of approximately 19; delta/phi = 0.44 with phi = 32 interpolates to R = 0.679 (Matrix 4-1: phi 30, 32, 35 deg against delta/phi 0.5, 0.44, 0.4 = 0.746/0.710/0.686, 0.717/0.679/0.653, 0.674/0.631/0.603); Kp' = R Kp = 0.679(19) = 13.
key_points: Rankine's theory should not be used for passive pressure on shoring (it does not account for wall friction)
Coulomb passive grows increasingly erroneous as wall friction increases and could lead to unsafe designs
Figure 4-20 (Caquot & Kerisel 1948), granular soils: initial Kp from phi and beta/phi
Reduction factor R from delta/phi and phi (Matrix 4-1); final Kp' = R x Kp
Conditions outside Figure 4-20: a trial wedge or logarithmic spiral procedure may be used
Example: phi=32, beta/phi=0.84 -> Kp~19; delta/phi=0.44 -> R=0.679; Kp'=13

equations.description: Final log-spiral passive coefficient Kp' = R * Kp (R from Matrix 4-1, Kp from Figure 4-20).
